experiment.elements-plus.group.intro.sec: Welcome to the ElementsPlus Experiment Table!
Here you can test your own circuits and gradually unlock various advanced components.
Insert your circuit diagram into the slot above and click the "Start Experiment" button, and the experiment will be automatically performed.

After the experiment is successful, you will obtain a compiled circuit diagram, which is associated with a component. It can be used directly as a component in the lithography machine, or used in the "Manufacture" tab of the lithography machine to manufacture chips.

Note: Compiled circuit diagrams cannot be edited further, but you can create a copy of the circuit diagram in the lithography machine manufacturing page, and uncheck the "Keep Compiled" option. The copy will no longer have the compiled status and can be edited further.

If the experiment fails, the progress bar will turn red, and hovering over it will show the specific failure reason. The state of the input components in the circuit diagram will be frozen at the failed test case, and you can view the specific failure logic by placing it in the lithography machine later.
That's all to be introduced, start your experiment journey now, have fun!
experiment.elements-plus.group.amplifier: Signals have 0~15 strengths in total, but we mostly focus on "yes" and "no".

To achieve this, we introduce a simple component - the %s. As long as the input signal strength is greater than 0, the output signal strength is 15. Thus, we can focus on higher-level logic without worrying about the details.
To achieve this, we need a component that can amplify the signal strength. And that is the %s.

A transistor is a component that can amplify signals. When there is no input on the side, it can amplify the input on the front by two times. (Side input will be mentioned later, this experiment does not require it)
Now, try to use this property to complete the experiment.
Input A, as long as A is non-zero, output Y=15, otherwise output Y=0.

Please build the circuit in the lithography machine, and place the circuit diagram into the slot above after completion. Click the "Start Experiment" button, and the experiment will be automatically performed.
You should see below the "Test Information" appear multiple boxes, each corresponding to a test case. The text above the test case means:
• %s: Test is still running (you will see in the sequential logic that will be introduced later)
experiment.elements-plus.group.first_gat: First Gate
Good job, you should now have passed your first experiment and obtained a compiled circuit diagram.
A compiled circuit diagram can be used directly as a component in the lithography machine design page, and you can also add it to the component list.
You should have already noticed the lithography machine manufacturing page, and it is now time to understand how to use it.
The lithography machine manufacturing page can copy circuits, manufacture chips and circuit boards.

If you want to copy a circuit, please place the circuit in the first slot as a template, and the second slot with the uncompiled circuit to be covered. At this time, a copy of the template circuit will appear in the output slot. Take it away, and the template will not be consumed, and the second slot circuit will be consumed. (Note: This operation will permanently cover the second slot circuit, and it is recommended to use an empty circuit)

If you want to make a chip, please place the compiled circuit diagram in the first grid as a template, and place the empty chip that %s in the second grid. At this time, the raw materials required for making the chip will be displayed.
greater than or equal to circuit diagram scale
Among them,
• Basic components usually need the corresponding amethyst component items
• Advanced components need corresponding chips of any scale (manufactured by this method)
• Wires need corresponding block number of %s and %s items (bus multiplied by bit width)
• Input/output and bus joiner/splitter does not require raw materials
When all raw materials are satisfied in the inventory, a chip will appear in the output slot. Take it away, and the empty chip and raw materials will be deducted.
Now that we have learned how to make chips, we will move on to making the first logic gate.

We have already introduced the amplification function of transistors, and now we introduce the side input of transistors. The side input will make the output linearly decay. 0 corresponds to 100% output, and 15 corresponds to 0% output (that is, completely shutting down the output).
If you are more comfortable using formulas, then in other words: the final output ratio of the transistor is %s. That is, the output is %s.
2*(1-side_input/15)
2*front_input*(1-side_input/15)

This time, we are going to design the component "%s". It is very simple——it has only one input and one output. You just need to ensure that it outputs 15 when the input is 0, and outputs 0 when the input is not 0.
NOT Gate
Hint: When the input is 0, the component cannot produce a signal out of thin air. Think of which basic component can produce a signal continuously?
In fact, with this component, you can create any complex %s.
combinational logic circuit

What we call a %s is a digital circuit whose output depends only on the current input state and not on the past state of the circuit. If you understand this, then congratulations, you still have some basic knowledge. If you find it difficult to understand, that's okay, you will gradually understand it later.
combinational logic circuit
If you think it's too simple, here's a challenge for you: design a component that outputs %s. We call it the "%s".
15-input
Analog NOT Gate
This experiment is optional, you can continue to the next chapter and come back to do it later.
experiment.elements-plus.group.basic_gat: Now that we have built our first logic gate, let's move on to building more logic gates.
This chapter's logic gates will no longer have only one input, but usually have A and B two inputs.
• %s: If any input is non-zero, it outputs 15, otherwise it outputs 0.
• %s: If both inputs are non-zero, it outputs 15, otherwise it outputs 0.
• %s: If any input is non-zero, it outputs 0, otherwise it outputs 15.
• %s: If both inputs are non-zero, it outputs 0, otherwise it outputs 15.
Hint: NOR gate and NAND gate are not always just OR gate and AND gate with an additional NOT gate. For example, NAND gate actually needs fewer transistors than AND gate.
In the following chapters, we will frequently use these basic logic gates.
Additionally, this chapter also has an optional challenge:
• %s: If A is non-zero, output B, otherwise output A
• %s: If A is zero, output B, otherwise output A
experiment.elements-plus.group.advanced_: I'm sure you're already intimidated by the high cost of batteries, but it's okay. You don't need or recommend having a built-in battery for every chip - the chips you want to manufacture in the future will require more and more sub chips, and this "built-in battery" design will undoubtedly increase costs exponentially.

The experiment table will provide an additional optional input, "VCC", which you can connect to any pin of your circuit, and it will automatically receive a signal strength of 15. The VCC pin will not be explicitly exposed on the component; they will be implicitly connected to the outer layer one by one, so you only need one battery to power the entire machine.
You can also follow the same design when designing circuits: do not built-in batteries, but reserve input interfaces instead, which can significantly reduce the demand for batteries!
After making the basic logic gates, let's move on to two more advanced logic gates. These gates also have A and B two inputs and Y one output.
• %s: Odd number of inputs non-zero, output 15; even number of inputs non-zero, output 0.
• %s: Odd number of inputs non-zero, output 0; even number of inputs non-zero, output 15.
You can try to solve it by combining the logic gates you have unlocked before.

After completing these chapters, you can directly jump to “%s”, but it is recommended that you complete these chapters as soon as possible, as they can provide a lot of help in your future design. Moreover, they are prerequisite chapters for some optional chapters.
experiment.elements-plus.group.three_way: We have already built some logic gates, and sometimes we need to handle data that is three or more. By connecting two components in series, we can achieve this, but we can also integrate it into a more efficient component.
In this experiment, we will build a three-way logic gate, which takes inputs A, B, and C, and produces an output Y:
• %s: If any one of the inputs is non-zero, it outputs 15, otherwise it outputs 0.
• %s: If all three inputs are non-zero, it outputs 15, otherwise it outputs 0.
• %s: If an odd number of inputs are non-zero, it outputs 15; if an even number of inputs are non-zero, it outputs 0.
• %s: If an odd number of inputs are non-zero, it outputs 0; if an even number of inputs are non-zero, it outputs 15.
This chapter is optional, you can choose to directly proceed to the next chapter, but completing this chapter first may be helpful for your future design.
experiment.elements-plus.group.one_bit_a: Have you ever wondered how we represent numbers in circuits?
Indeed, the signal strength of 0~15 can represent 16 numbers. However, signal strength also has its drawbacks: it is difficult to read and process, and it will attenuate in macro circuits.
To address this, we will introduce a more stable and easy-to-use number representation method——%s.

The numbers we use daily are base 10 (%s), which means we carry over every 10. Binary, on the other hand, is base 2, meaning each digit in a binary number can only be 0 or 1. When 1+1, it equals (10)₂. This way, we can represent a binary number using multiple wires, and we don't care about the signal strength of each digit, only whether it 'has' or 'does not have' a signal, corresponding to 1 and 0 respectively.
In this experiment, we will handle the addition of one-bit binary numbers. First, we need to do the addition of two one-bit binary numbers. This component is called the “%s”.
• %s: Inputs A and B, add A and B as binary numbers (non-zero corresponds to 1, zero corresponds to 0), output sum S and carry C (1 corresponds to 15, 0 corresponds to 0).
To make it more intuitive, we list all the cases of the half adder below:

Handling the addition of two one-bit binary numbers is not enough, because if we want to perform addition of multi-bit binary numbers, we need to handle the carry problem. Therefore, we need to handle the addition of three-bit binary numbers, which is called the “%s”.
• %s: Inputs A, B, and CI, add A and B as binary numbers (non-zero corresponds to 1, zero corresponds to 0), output sum S and carry CO (1 corresponds to 15, 0 corresponds to 0).

experiment.elements-plus.group.multi_bit: Now we will implement the addition of multi-bit binary numbers.
In this chapter, we introduce the concept of %s. Bus is actually a bundle of multiple wires, which simplifies the wiring and allows you to avoid the trouble of arranging multiple parallel wires.

The number on the right side of the wire button in the lithography machine tool bar is the current bit width. You can click or scroll the mouse wheel on it to switch the bit width. The bus will no longer change color according to the signal strength, but will display a fixed color corresponding to the bus bit width. Only wires with matching bit width can be connected to certain component pins.
Find “%s” and “%s”, as well as “%s” and “%s” in the component list. We will use them in this chapter.
We unify the rules for bus joiners and splitters, specifying that the side closer to the opposite pin (the upper side when placed upright) is the least significant bit.

In the previous chapter, you already made a component that can handle the addition of one-bit binary numbers. We can recall the process of calculating the addition by column: the carry is placed in the high position as the addend. This is also applicable to binary numbers.
In this experiment, we will build a “%s”: it accepts two 8-bit binary numbers and a carry input, and outputs an 8-bit binary number sum and a 1-bit carry output.
• %s: Inputs A (8-bit), B (8-bit), CI (1-bit). Add them as binary numbers and output the sum S (8-bit) and carry output CO (1-bit).
